The details

The 4 mattress types, without the sales talk

Almost every mattress is one of these — or a mix. Learn the type first; brand names come second.

Best for pressure relief

Memory foam

Foam that softens with body heat and moulds around shoulders and hips. The classic “hug” feeling, and the strongest motion isolation if your partner tosses and turns.

  • Feels: slow, contouring, quiet — you sleep in it, not on it
  • Thickness tip: look for 10–12″ with at least 2–3″ of comfort foam on top
  • Good first look if: you are a side sleeper with sore shoulders
✓ Strength

Best shoulder & hip relief; near-silent for couples

✕ Watch out

Can sleep warm and feel hard to roll over on

Soft
Firm
Best all-rounder · Most couples agree on this

Hybrid

Coils underneath, foam or latex on top. You get bounce and airflow from the springs with cushioning from the comfort layers — the easiest type to compromise on.

  • Feels: responsive, supportive, cooler than all-foam
  • What to check: individually pocketed coils + reinforced edges if you sit on the side
  • Good first look if: you switch positions or share the bed
✓ Strength

Balances support, cooling and bounce for most bodies

✕ Watch out

Heavier to move; quality varies a lot — check coil type

Soft
Firm
Best for hot sleepers · Longest lasting

Latex

Made from rubber-tree sap (natural) or a synthetic blend. Springy rather than sinking, naturally breathable, and usually the longest-lasting foam you can buy.

  • Feels: buoyant, quick to respond, cool — you sleep on it
  • What to check: natural vs. blend, and whether layers are Dunlop (firmer) or Talalay (softer)
  • Good first look if: you sleep hot and dislike the foam “hug”
✓ Strength

Coolest foam feel + holds its shape for years

✕ Watch out

Higher price; very heavy in King sizes — plan delivery

Soft
Firm
Best on a budget · Best airflow

Innerspring

The traditional coil mattress with a thinner comfort layer. Familiar bounce, strong airflow, and often the lowest price — especially in guest rooms and kids’ rooms.

  • Feels: bouncy, firm, cool, easy to move on
  • Smart upgrade: add a 2″ topper for pressure relief instead of replacing it early
  • Good first look if: you are a stomach sleeper or furnishing a spare room
✓ Strength

Lowest entry price, coolest traditional feel

✕ Watch out

Less pressure relief; can creak and transfer motion

Decode the label

Firmness, translated: what 1–10 actually feels like

There is no industry standard — one brand's “medium” is another's “firm.” Use this scale as a common language, then adjust for your body: heavier sleepers feel a bed softer, lighter sleepers feel it firmer.

1 — Cloud-soft5–6 — True medium (most people)10 — Floor-firm
Soft · 3–4 / 10

Deep sink, strong hug. Best for lighter side sleepers and sore joints. Too soft for stomach sleepers — hips dip and backs ache.

Medium to medium-firm · 5–7 / 10

The sweet spot for most back, side and combo sleepers — and almost every couple compromise. If unsure, start here.

Firm · 7.5–9 / 10

Minimal sink, you float on top. Best for stomach sleepers, heavier back sleepers, and anyone who hates feeling “stuck.”

In-store test that actually works: lie in your real sleep position for a full 10–15 minutes — not 30 seconds on your back. For side sleeping, your spine should look straight from behind; for back sleeping, slide a hand under your lower back — slight resistance is right, a big gap is too firm, no gap is too soft.

Step 3 — Your position

Match the bed to how you sleep

Your sleep position decides where your weight lands — and that decides how firm your mattress should be.

◐

Side sleepers

Your shoulder and hip carry most of your weight. Go soft to medium so those joints can sink in and your spine stays straight. A pillow between the knees helps more than most people expect.

Target: 3–5.5 / 10 · Thicker pillow
◒

Back sleepers

You need support under the lower back more than cushioning. Medium to medium-firm is the sweet spot — soft enough to feel comfortable, firm enough that your hips don’t dip.

Target: 5.5–7 / 10 · Medium pillow
◑

Stomach sleepers

A soft bed lets your midsection sink and strains your back. Choose firm, and use a thin pillow — or none — so your neck isn’t cranked upward all night.

Target: 7–9 / 10 · Thin or no pillow
↻

Combination sleepers & couples

If you roll between positions, or share with someone who sleeps differently, a medium hybrid is the safest compromise: responsive when you move, quiet when they do.

Target: 5.5–6.5 / 10 · Responsive hybrid
Don't buy the wrong size

Mattress sizes — exact dimensions, honest advice

US standard sizes. Measure your frame's inside dimensions before ordering — European and IKEA sizes differ, and “Queen” is not the same everywhere.

Twin
38″ × 75″ · 97 × 191 cm

Kids, teens, and single sleepers in tight rooms. Too short for most adults over 6′.

Twin XL
38″ × 80″ · 97 × 203 cm

Same width, adult length. Two side-by-side = a King — the classic adjustable / split-King setup.

Full / Double
54″ × 75″ · 137 × 191 cm

Roomy for one, snug for two. A good guest-room and first-apartment pick.

Queen — most popular
60″ × 80″ · 152 × 203 cm

The default couple size for most bedrooms. Fits rooms from about 10′ × 10′ up comfortably.

King
76″ × 80″ · 193 × 203 cm

Each partner gets a Twin XL of space. Needs a larger room and two people (or delivery help) to move.

California King
72″ × 84″ · 183 × 213 cm

Narrower but 4″ longer than a King — for tall sleepers, not for maximum width. Bedding is harder to find.

Rule of thumb: leave at least 24–30″ of walking space on each side you use. If a King forces you to shuffle sideways, a Queen will sleep better in that room.

Step 4 — The other half of sleep

Sleep essentials that earn their place

A great mattress does half the job. These layers and small fixes do the other half — in the order we would buy them, cheapest high-impact fixes included.

  • 1
    The right pillow for your positionThicker for side sleepers, medium for back sleepers, thin for stomach sleepers. If you wake with a sore neck, change this before the mattress.Fix this first — it's the cheapest change with the biggest payoff
  • 2
    A washable mattress protectorQuiet, waterproof, and not plasticky. It protects your warranty as much as your mattress — many warranties are voided by stains.Buy on day one, with the mattress
  • 3
    Breathable sheets — two setsCotton percale if you sleep hot, sateen or washed linen if you like a softer, warmer feel. Two sets, so laundry day never strips the bed.
  • 4
    A layer you can kick offA light throw or muslin blanket at the foot of the bed lets you adjust temperature at 2 a.m. without remaking the whole bed.
  • 5
    Real darknessBlackout curtains or a simple sleep mask. Street light through thin curtains is one of the cheapest sleep problems to fix.
  • 6
    Warm, low light at nightA small warm-toned bedside lamp instead of the ceiling light for the last hour. It makes the room feel cozy and signals wind-down time.
Spend it in the right order

How to split a sleep budget (without overspending)

We don't list prices here because they change by country, sale and retailer — but the proportions hold almost everywhere. Put the money where your body actually touches the bed.

If your total sleep budget is 100%, aim roughly for:
~60% — Mattress + base

The support layer. Never save money here by downgrading the base — a great mattress on a sagging base feels like a bad mattress.

~25% — Pillow + protector + sheets

The comfort layer you feel directly. Two sheet sets and the right pillow beat one luxury duvet set every time.

~15% — Darkness + light + throw

Blackout, warm lamp, kick-off layer. Small spend, outsized effect on how fast you fall asleep.

Where NOT to spend first: decorative cushions, a headboard upgrade, or a thicker duvet — all lovely later, none of them fix a sore back or a hot night. And beware “sale” pricing: compare the same model's everyday price across two retailers before calling anything a deal.

Step 5 — Final checks

Before you buy, do these 5 things

Five minutes of checking now prevents the most common — and most expensive — mattress mistakes.

1

Measure your frame, not your old mattress

Frames vary. Measure the inside of your bed frame and check the new mattress dimensions against the size guide above — especially with platform and storage beds. Check doorways and stairs for King deliveries too.

2

Read the trial & return terms on the retailer’s own page

Trial lengths, return pickups and fees change often and differ by brand. Check them on the seller’s site on the day you buy, and keep a screenshot with your order confirmation.

3

Check what base it needs

Foam and hybrid mattresses usually need a solid or closely-slatted base. Wide-spaced slats or an old box spring can void the warranty and ruin the feel — ask before, not after delivery.

4

Give it a real adjustment period

A new mattress — and your body — need time. Most brands ask for a few weeks before a return, and most sleepers are glad they waited. Judge it after 2–3 weeks, not night one.

5

Budget for the protector on day one

It is the cheapest insurance in the whole purchase: it keeps the mattress clean, the trial valid, and the warranty intact.

And avoid these 3 expensive mistakes

✕

Buying firmness by the label

“Medium-firm” means something different at every brand. Shop by the 1–10 target from your matcher result and your sleep position — not the word on the tag.

✕

Testing for 30 seconds, fully dressed, on your back

That tells you almost nothing. Lie in your real position for 10–15 minutes, or rely on a proper home trial with free returns.

✕

Replacing the mattress when the pillow is the problem

Neck pain, headaches and shoulder numbness are very often pillow-height problems. Try the pillow fix first — it's a fraction of the cost.

Quick questions, straight answers

The questions every mattress shopper asks — answered without pushing a brand. Still unsure? Run the matcher again with your partner's answers and meet in the middle (usually: medium hybrid).

Re-run the matcher ↑
How firm should my mattress be?

Start from your sleep position: soft-to-medium (3–5.5/10) for side sleepers, medium to medium-firm (5.5–7/10) for back sleepers, firm (7–9/10) for stomach sleepers. Body weight shifts it too — heavier sleepers usually need one step firmer, lighter sleepers one step softer.

Memory foam or hybrid — which is better?

Neither, in general. Memory foam wins on pressure relief and motion isolation; hybrids win on airflow, bounce and edge support. If you sleep hot or share the bed with a restless partner, that trade-off matters more than any brand comparison.

We sleep differently — what should a couple buy?

A medium hybrid (around 6/10) with pocketed coils is the safest shared compromise. If you differ a lot, look at split-firmness models, or two Twin XLs on a King frame so each side can be different.

How long should a mattress last?

Most mattresses perform well for roughly 7–10 years depending on type and care. Latex tends to last longest, budget innersprings the shortest. Rotating the mattress head-to-foot every few months and using a protector extends any of them. Replace it when you see visible sagging, feel the base, or wake up sore more mornings than not.

Do I need a new base or bed frame too?

Only if yours sags, creaks, or has wide-spaced slats. Foam and hybrids need solid or closely-spaced support (slats roughly 3″ apart or less is a common brand requirement — check yours). A failing base makes even a great new mattress feel wrong.

I can only change one thing — where do I start?

The pillow, if your neck hurts. The protector, if your mattress is new. Blackout curtains, if your room never gets dark. The mattress itself only when it sags, creaks, or you wake up sore more mornings than not.
